Statement

Semi-Annual Virtual and On-Site Safety Audit Report 6 (“Audit Report 6”) of the Metro Denver 
area Regional Transportation District (“RTD”) light rail operation filed on December 29, 2025.

on-site safety review of RTD’s Public Transportation Agency Safety Plan as required by 
Rule 7360 of the Rules Regulating Railroads, Rail Fixed Guideways, Transportation by Rail, and 
Rail Crossings, 5 Code of Colorado Regulations 723-7. Commission Safety Audit Rule 7360 was 
completed by Staff of the Commission (“Staff”). There are no findings made during the sixth audit 
of the cycle. 
3.

Report 6. RTD’s comments were prepared and submitted to address the findings found during the

title: Colorado PUC Decision R26-0019-I: Interim Decision Denying Motion for Summary Judgment
summary: Interim Decision Denying Motion for Summary Judgment
text:
Decision No. R26-0019-I 
BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF COLORADO 
PROCEEDING NO. 25F-0436EG 
DWIGHT BORDELON, 

COMPLAINANT, 
V. 
PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY OF COLORADO., 

RESPONDENT. 
INTERIM DECISION 
DENYING MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT 
Issued Date: January 9, 2026 
I. 
STATEMENT 
A. 
Procedural Background 
1. 
On October 17, 2025, Complainant Dwight Bordelon filed a Complaint against Public 
Service Company of Colorado (“Public Service” or “the Company”). Mr. Bordelon generally alleges 
that Public Service failed to change his electric service from Time of Use (“RE-TOU”) rate schedule to 
Residential Opt Out (“R-OO”) rate schedule within 30 days. 
2. 
On October 21, 2025, the Commission issued its Order Setting Hearing and Notice of 
Hearing (“Notice”), which set this matter for an evidentiary hearing on January 5, 2026, before an 
Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”). 
Colorado PUC E-Filings System

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. R26-0019-I 
Proceeding No. 25F-0436EG 
2 
3. 
On October 29, 2025, the above captioned proceeding was referred by minute entry to an 
ALJ. 
4. 
On November 10, 2025, Public Service filed its Answer. 
5. 
On November 18, 2025, by Decision No. R25-0821-I, a prehearing conference was 
scheduled for December 11, 2025. 
6. 
On December 9, 2025, Public Service filed its Motion to Dismiss. 
7. 
On December 11, 2025, a prehearing conference was held. 
8. 
On December 11, 2025, Complainant filed a Motion for an Extension to File Response 
(“Motion for Extension”). 
9. 
On December 17, 2025, by Decision No. R25-0904-I a procedural schedule was adopted, 
and the evidentiary hearing was rescheduled for February 3, 2026. 
10. 
On December 22, 2025, by Decision No. R25-0922-I, the Motion for Extension was 
granted. 
11. 
On December 30, 2025, Complainant filed his Response to Request for Summary 
Judgement (“Response”). 
I. 
MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT 
A. 
Argument of Public Service 
12. 
Public Service argues that the Complainant alleges that he was billed incorrectly under 
the RE-TOU rate schedule when he should have been billed under the R-OO rate schedule. 
13. 
Public Service provides an affidavit and billing statements that it asserts show that the 
Complainant was billed correctly. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. R26-0019-I 
Proceeding No. 25F-0436EG 
3 
14. 
Public Service states that since there is no genuine dispute of material facts the Company 
is entitled to summary judgment and dismissal of the Formal Complaint as a matter of law1. 
B. 
Response of Complainant 
15. 
Complainant argues that Public Service failed to change his rate plan from RE-TOU to 
R-OO within the thirty-day period required under their tariff. 
16. 
Complainant states that he was uncertain which rate plan he was on, potentially creating 
an overpayment of $28.802. 
17. 
Complainant also states that Public Service lacks clarity on its webpage and “fails to meet 
PUC requirements for informational accuracy.3” 
II. 
DISCUSSION 
A. 
Applicable Law 
18. 
The complaint in the instant case is filed pursuant to § 40-15-115, C.R.S.: 

(1)(a) Complaint may be made by the commission on its own motion or by 
any corporation, person, chamber of commerce, or board of trade, or by 
any civic, commercial, mercantile, traffic, agricultural, or manufacturing 
association or organization, or by any body politic or municipal 
corporation by petition or complaint in writing, setting forth any act or 
thing done or omitted to be done by any public utility, including any rule, 
regulation, or charge heretofore established or fixed by or for any public 
utility, in violation, or claimed to be in violation, of any provision of law 
or of any order or rule of the commission. 

(b) No complaint shall be entertained by the commission, except upon its 
own motion, as to the reasonableness of any rates or charges of any gas, 
electric, water, or telephone public utility, unless the same is signed by the 
mayor or the president or chairman of the board of trustees or a majority 
of the council, commission, or other legislative body of the county, city 
and county, city, or town, if any, within which the alleged violation 

1 Motion to Dismiss, p.5. 
2 Response, p. 3. 
3 Response, p,2 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. R26-0019-I 
Proceeding No. 25F-0436EG 
4 
occurred, or not less than twenty-five customers or prospective customers 
of such public utility. 
19. 
Rule 1400(f) of the Rules of Practice and Procedure, 4 CCR 723-1, permits summary 
judgment motions filed in accordance with Rule 56, Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure 
(C.R.C.P.). Summary judgment is proper when the moving party can demonstrate that “there is no 
genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of 
law.” Rule 56(c), C.R.C.P. 
20. 
The Colorado Supreme Court has summarized the principles applicable to ruling on 
motions for summary judgment: 
Summary judgment is a drastic remedy and should only be granted if there 
is a clear showing that no genuine issue as to any material fact exists and the 
moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. See C.R.C.P. 56; 
Greenwood Trust Co. v. Conley, 938 P.2d 1141, 1149 (Colo. 1997). The 
moving party has the initial burden to show that there is no genuine issue of 
material fact. See Greenwood Trust, 938 P.2d at 1149. Once the moving 
party has met its initial burden, the burden shifts to the nonmoving party to 
establish that there is a triable issue of fact. See id. The nonmoving party is 
entitled to all favorable inferences that may be drawn from the undisputed 
facts, and all doubts as to whether a triable issue of fact exists must be 
resolved against the moving party. See Bayou Land Co. v. Talley, 924 P.2d 
136, 151 (Colo. 1996). 
21. 
A fact is “material,” for purposes of a motion for summary judgment, if 
it will affect the outcome of the case. Gadlin v. Metrex Research Corporation, 76 P.3d 928 (Colo. App. 
2003). Summary judgment is appropriate when the pleadings and supporting documents demonstrate 
that no genuine issue as to any material fact exists and that the moving party is entitled to summary 
judgment as a matter of law. Martini v. Smith, 42 P.3d 629 (Colo. 2002). 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. R26-0019-I 
Proceeding No. 25F-0436EG 
5 
B. 
Motion for Summary Judgment 
22. 
A complaint may be filed by a person alleging the failure to do or not do setting forth any 
act or thing done or omitted to be done by any public utility, including any rule, regulation, or charge. 
§ 40-15-115, C.R.S (1)(a). 
23. 
The Complaint alleges that Public Service failed to switch the Complainant to the R-OO 
rate plan within 30 days, which resulted in excessive charges4. The Complainant does not state any rule 
or regulation that Public Service has allegedly violated.5 
24. 
The scope of this Complainant is limited to determining if the Complainant was switched 
to the R-OO rate plan within 30 days. 
25. 
Public Service has provided evidence that the Complainant was switched to the R-OO 
rate plan within 30 days. With this showing by Public Service, the burden then shifts to the Complainant 
to establish that there is a triable issue of fact. 
26. 
The Complainant has provided screen captures and chat/phone transcripts that are to an 
extent confusing or could be construed as confusing as to when the Complainant was placed on the 
R-OO rate plan. 
27. 
The date the Complainant was switched to the R-OO rate is a material fact. There is a 
dispute as to whether the change in rate plans was accomplished within 30 days and if there were 
excessive charges up to $28.80. 
28. 
Since a material fact is in dispute, the Motion for Summary Judgment fails. 

4 The Complainant argues this may have led to an overcharge of up to $28.80. Response p. 3. The 
Complainant does not allege that Public Service has continued to bill the Complainant under the R-TOU rate plan 
beyond November of 2025. 
5 There are references made in the Response to a failure to serve the public interest in a variety of ways 
but the Complainant does not list any rule or regulation that Public Service is alleged to have violated. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. R26-0019-I 
Proceeding No. 25F-0436EG 
6 
III. 
ORDER 
A. 
It Is Ordered That: 
1. 
The Motion for Summary Judgment filed by Public Service Company of Colorado on 
December 9, 2025, is denied. 
2. 
The above captioned Complaint remains scheduled for an evidentiary hearing 
commencing at 9:00 am on February 3, 2026. 
3. 
The Parties shall be held to the advisements in this Decision. 
4. 
This Decision shall be effective immediately. 

(S E A L)

Rebecca E. White, 
Director 
THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION 
OF THE STATE OF COLORADO 

ROBERT I. GARVEY 
________________________________ 
Administrative Law Judge

title: Colorado PUC Decision C26-0041: Commission Decision Denying Temporary Authority
text:
Decision No. C26-0041 
BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF COLORADO 
PROCEEDING NO. 26A-0033CP-ETA 
IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF EMERALD EXPRESS TRANSPORTATION, 
INC. FOR EMERGENCY TEMPORARY AUTHORITY TO OPERATE AS A COMMON 
CARRIER BY MOTOR VEHICLE FOR HIRE. 
COMMISSION DECISION DENYING 
TEMPORARY AUTHORITY 
Issued Date: 
January 16, 2026 
Adopted Date: January 14, 2026 

I. 
BY THE COMMISSION 
A. 
Statement, Findings, and Conclusions 
1. 
On January 5, 2025, Emerald Express Transportation, Inc. (“Emerald Express”) 
filed an Application for Emergency Temporary Authority1 to Operate as a Common Carrier of 
Passengers by Motor Vehicle for Hire (“Application”). 
2. 
Emerald Express, in this Application, requests emergency temporary authority for 
30 days as follows: 
(1) Transportation of passengers in call-and-demand shuttle service 
between all points within the city of Steamboat Springs, Colorado, and 
between said points, on the one hand, and the Yampa Valley Regional 
Airport, Hayden, Colorado, on the other hand. (2) Transportation of 
passengers in call-and-demand shuttle service between all points within the 

1 Emerald Express Transportation filed an Application for a Certificate of Public Convenience and 
Necessity to operate as a common carrier of passengers on May 19, 2025, in Proceeding 25A-0202CP. 
The permanent authority requested in Proceeding 25A-0202CP is the same as in Proceeding 
26A-0033CP-ETA. Alpine Taxi/Limo, Inc. and NDW Enterprises LLC, doing business as Ski Town 
Transportation, filed Interventions by Right to the permanent authority application. An evidentiary hearing 
was scheduled for December 2-4, 2025, by Decision No. R25-0778-I. As of January 14, 2026, the 
administrative law judge assigned to o Proceeding 25A-0202CP has not issued a recommended decision 
granting or denying the permanent application. 
Colorado PUC E-Filings System

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0041 
PROCEEDING NO. 26A-0033CP-ETA 
2 
city of Craig, Colorado, and between said points, on the one hand, and the 
Yampa Valley Regional Airport, Hayden, Colorado, on the other hand. 
3. 
Pursuant to § 40-10.1-204(1), C.R.S., the Commission is authorized to grant 
temporary authority when “there appears to be an immediate and urgent need to any point or within 
a territory having no such service capable of meeting the need.” Section 40-10.1-204(4), C.R.S., 
further states: “If the Commission determines that an emergency exists, it may issue temporary 
authority or approval at once by making specific reference in its order to the circumstances 
constituting the emergency, in which case no notice need be given, but any such emergency 
authority or approval expires no later than thirty days after it was issued.” 
4. 
Therefore, Emerald Express must meet a two-fold test: first, that there is an 
immediate and urgent need for the transportation services, and second, that there is no existing 
carrier capable of meeting the need. If Emerald Express fails to meet either test, the Application 
must be denied. 
5. 
Rule 6204(b) of the Rules Regulating Transportation by Motor Vehicle, 4 Code of 
Colorado Regulations (“CCR”) 723-6 states: 
(b) A Person may seek emergency temporary Authority to operate as a 
Common or Contract Carrier for a period not to exceed 30 days and shall 
file an application with the Commission providing the information in 
paragraph (a) of this rule. The application shall also include a statement of 
facts establishing the basis and nature of the emergency need for the 
proposed service. Any letters of support shall describe the basis and nature 
of the emergency. 
6. 
In support of the emergency temporary authority application, Emerald Express 
Transportation states the following: 
Yampa Valley Regional Airport (“YVRA” or the “Airport”) is a critical 
regional transportation hub that provides year-round commercial air 
service, business jet operations, general aviation access, air cargo, and 
medical evacuation support for Northwest Colorado communities, 
including Steamboat Springs and Craig. Since 2021, YVRA has 
experienced sustained and unprecedented growth in commercial airline 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0041 
PROCEEDING NO. 26A-0033CP-ETA 
3 
traffic. Six major airlines now provide direct winter-season flights between 
YBRA and sixteen major U.S. airports, resulting in significant increases in 
total passenger volume, including during the current winter season both at 
present and anticipated. This rapid and significant expansion has increased 
the public need for and reliance on ground transportation from the resort 
community of Steamboat Springs, as well as the need for transportation to 
and from Craig (where many local workers reside). Recently, one of the two 
existing CPCN holders serving the YVRA in call and demand shuttle 
service (i.e. providing “walk up” transportation), Alpine Taxi/Limo 
(aka Steamboat Express) was banned from serving the Airport after it a) 
pulled out of its counter service and b) became embroiled in a contract 
dispute with the Airport. Alpine was also, on information and belief, 
suffering from operational and financial instability. Alpine has represented 
that it does not intend to re-open a counter at YVRA, and it is currently 
involved in a dispute before the PUC regarding its ban from Airport 
premises, but by its own admission it is currently unable to serve the 
YVRA2. As a result, only one certified ground transportation provider 
remains available to meet the needs of thousands of arriving and departing 
passengers each week. 
7. 
The CEO, Sarah Leonard, of the Steamboat Springs Chamber wrote a letter of 
support for Emerald Express’ ETA application on December 17, 2025. In the letter Ms. Leonard 
states: 
On behalf of the Steamboat Springs Chamber, I’m writing to share our 
formal support for Emerald Express Transportation’s request for 
Emergency and Temporary Common Carrier Authority. With winter air 
service already begun, our community is facing an immediate and 
significant shortage of walk-up ground transportation at the Yampa Valley 
Regional Airport (YVRA) making this request time sensitive for our 
community. As we noted in our earlier correspondence and outlined in my 
recent testimony on behalf of Emerald Express in Proceeding 24A-0202CP, 
the closure of Alpine Taxi/Limo (aka Steamboat Express)’s airport 
operations created a substantial gap in shared transportation options for 
residents and visitors flying into YVRA. Today, only one authorized walk-
up provider remains at YVRA—an arrangement that currently does not 

2 Alpine Taxi/Limo, Inc. ("Alpine Taxi") filed a Petition for Declaratory Order ("Petition") with 
the Colorado Public Utility Commission (“Commission”) on October 15, 2025. In the Petition, Alpine Taxi 
is seeking an order from the Commission addressing whether Yampa Valley Regional Airport (“YVRA”) 
has the authority to bar Alpine Taxi from serving YVRA. The Commission accepted the Petition and 
referred it to an administrative law judge by Decision C25-0791 on November 4, 2025, in Proceeding No. 
25D-0435CP. On December 4, 2025, Routt County filed a Motion to Intervene of Right or in the Alternative 
Motion for Leave to Intervene. Routt County was acknowledged as a party of right on December 22, 2025, 
in Decision No. R25-0920-I. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0041 
PROCEEDING NO. 26A-0033CP-ETA 
4 
meet the needs of winter travelers, particularly during peak arrival windows 
and challenging weather. Reliable airport transportation is an essential part 
of the Steamboat Springs visitor experience. Our hotels, restaurants, 
retailers, event venues, and local businesses depend on safe, predictable 
access for guests and employees alike. When ground transportation falls 
short, those impacts ripple throughout our community, affecting visitor 
satisfaction, reliability, and the overall strength of our economy. Steamboat 
Springs relies on positive experiences and return visitation to sustain our 
busy winter season. 
8. 
The Commission is aware that NDW Enterprises, LLC doing business as Ski Town 
Transportation (“Ski Town”) was issued Certificate No. 55991 on July 19, 2023, by Decision No. 
R23-0302 in Proceeding No. 22A-0132CP. Certificate No. 55991 authorizes Ski Town to provide 
shuttle service (a) between the YRVA and all points in Steamboat Springs, Colorado and all points 
within one mile of the city limits of Steamboat Springs; and (b) between the YRVA and all points 
in Craig, Colorado. 
9. 
The Commission is also aware that Steamboat Shuttle Service, LLC, doing 
business as Steamboat Shuttle Service (“Steamboat Shuttle Service”) was granted authority on 
December 19, 2025, to provide call-and demand shuttle service and call-and-demand charter 
service between all points in Routt County by Decision No. C25-0914 in Proceeding 25A-0454CP. 
Steamboat Shuttle Service has not completed the compliance requirements named in Decision No. 
C25-0914. The Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (“CPCN”) to operate as a 
common carrier of passengers will not be issued to Steamboat Shuttle Service until the compliance 
requirements are completed. 
10. 
The Commission finds that while the statements provided by the owner of 
Emerald Express Transportation and the CEO of the Steamboat Springs Chamber may support the 
need for additional passenger carriers during the winter season, these statements do not meet the 
standards of showing an immediate and urgent need as required by § 40-10.1-204 (1), C.R.S and 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0041 
PROCEEDING NO. 26A-0033CP-ETA 
5 
an emergency need for the proposed service as required by Rule 6204(b), 4 CCR 723-6. 
Considering that there is common carrier service available within the requested geographic area 
and that Emerald Express has not shown an immediate and urgent need, the Commission finds that 
the information submitted with the Application does not support the granting of emergency 
temporary authority. Thus, this application for emergency temporary authority is not in the public 
interest and will be denied. 
11. 
The denial of this Application creates no presumption about the final disposition of 
a temporary or permanent authority application filed by Emerald Express. 
II. 
ORDER 
A. 
The Commission Orders That: 
1. 
The application for emergency temporary authority filed on January 5, 2026, by 
Emerald Express Transportation, Inc. is denied, consistent with the discussion above. 
2. 
The 20-day time period provided by § 40-6-114(1), C.R.S., to file an Application 
for Rehearing, Reargument, or Reconsideration shall begin on the first day following the effective 
date of this Decision. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0041 
PROCEEDING NO. 26A-0033CP-ETA 
6

This Decision is effective immediately upon its Issued Date.

Decision No. C26-0049 
BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF COLORADO 
PROCEEDING NO. 25F-0335EG 
NEVILLE RUSTOMJEE, 
COMPLAINANT,

COMMISSION DECISION REOPENING PROCEEDING 
AND REMANDING TO ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE 
Issued Date: 
January 21, 2026

I. 
BY THE COMMISSION 
A. 
Statement 
1. 
Through this Decision, the Commission, on its own motion pursuant to 
Rule 1504(b), 4 Code of Colorado Regulations (“CCR”) 723-1, reopens this Proceeding and 
remands the matter to the assigned Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”). 
2. 
Attached to this Decision as Attachment A is Neville Rustomjee’s (“Complainant”) 
Response to Public Service Company of Colorado’s (“Public Service” or the “Company”) 
Motion to Dismiss Formal Complaint with Prejudice (“Motion to Dismiss”) filed on 
August 27, 2025. Attachment A is entered into the record as evidence in this Proceeding. 
Colorado PUC E-Filings System

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0049 
PROCEEDING NO. 25F-0335EG 
2 
B. 
Background 
3. 
On August 11, 2025, the Complainant filed a Complaint against Public Service, 
initiating this Proceeding. The Complaint alleged, among other things, that Public Service sent a 
Notice of Disconnection despite all payments being up to date, and requested an order from the 
Commission prohibiting the disconnection of services to his home until resolution of the matter. 
Additionally, the Complaint included various questions addressed to both the Commission and the 
president of Public Service, with a request that they be answered prior to any hearing. 
4. 
On August 13, 2025, Staff of the Public Utilities Commission served a copy of the 
Complaint to Public Service, alongside an order requiring the Company to satisfy or answer the 
Complaint within 20 days, in accordance with § 40-6-108, C.R.S. An evidentiary hearing was 
scheduled for October 27, 2025. 
5. 
On August 27, 2025, the matter was referred by minute entry to an ALJ. 
6. 
On August 27, 2025, Public Service filed its Motion to Dismiss. Public Service 
argued the Complaint must be dismissed because it does not contain sufficient factual allegations 
(accepted as true) to support any plausible claim for relief and that the Complaint does not allege 
any act or omission on Public Service’s part that would violate any provision of law or any order 
or rule of the Commission. 
7. 
The Motion to Dismiss contained a Certificate of Service indicating that the 
document was served upon the Complainant via U.S. Mail. 
8. 
The assigned ALJ issued Decision No. R25-0702EG (“Recommended Decision”) 
on September 30, 2025, granting Public Service’s Motion to Dismiss. The ALJ stated the 
Complainant had failed to file a response and not requested additional time to file a response to 
Public Service’s Motion to Dismiss and therefore dismissed the Complaint with prejudice. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0049 
PROCEEDING NO. 25F-0335EG 
3 
9. 
On October 10, 2025, the Complainant filed exceptions to the Recommended 
Decision, asserting that Public Service’s Motion to Dismiss was not served via U.S. Mail and that 
no copy of the filing was received. The Complainant therefore requested the Recommended 
Decision be set aside and requested an opportunity to respond to the Motion to Dismiss. 
10. 
Public Service responded to the Complainant’s exceptions on October 14, 2025, 
explaining that, in investigating the Complainant’s exceptions, the mail department inadvertently 
did not send the Motion to Dismiss as indicated in the Certificate of Service. Public Service states 
this was unintentional and an administrative oversight, and that upon discovery it has taken action 
to ensure proper service to the Complainant. Given this, Public Service requested the Commission 
reopen the Proceeding to ensure the Complainant has sufficient opportunity to respond to the 
Company’s Motion to Dismiss. 
11. 
Through Decision No. C25-0774, issued October 27, 2025, the Commission 
granted the Complainant’s exceptions, in part, and reopened the Proceeding and remanded the 
matter to the assigned ALJ for further proceedings. 
12. 
Through Decision No. R25-0777-I, issued October 29, 2025, the assigned ALJ 
ordered Public Service to serve the Motion to Dismiss on the Complainant by November 10, 2025. 
The Complainant had until November 24, 2025, to file a response to the Motion to Dismiss. 
13. 
Public Service filed its Notice of Service on November 6, 2025, which indicated 
that the Motion to Dismiss was sent via certified mail and delivered to the Complainant on 
November 1, 2025. 
14. 
Upon not receiving any response from the Complainant, the ALJ, through Decision 
No. R25-0882, issued December 12, 2025, granted Public Service’s Motion to Dismiss and 
dismissed the Complaint with prejudice, and closed the Proceeding. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0049 
PROCEEDING NO. 25F-0335EG 
4 
15. 
Pursuant to § 40-6-109, C.R.S., Decision No. R25-0882 became a Commission 
Decision on January 1, 2026. 
C. 
Findings and Conclusions 
16. 
Through informal communications, the Commission has been made aware that the 
Complainant physically mailed a Response to the Company's Motion to Dismiss (“Response”) that 
was received by Public Service. The Certificate of Service contained in the Response indicates it 
has been sent via certified mail to the Director of the Commission. 
17. 
The Commission has not received the Complainant’s Response in the mail. 
Using the provided United States Postal Service tracking number,1 it appears the Response was 
delivered to a mailing address in Denver (though a specific address is not provided) on November 
26, 2025. We are unaware whether this Response ever arrived at the Commission. However, even 
if the Commission had received the Complainant’s Response, the filing would have been late as 
the tracking number indicates it was delivered two days after the November 24, 2025 filing 
deadline established in Decision No. R25-0777-I. 
18. 
Subsequently, and again through informal communications, the Commission was 
made aware of a letter from the Complainant which was mailed to and received by Public Service. 
This letter was addressed to the Commission and indicates the Complainant mailed the Response 
to the Commission, has since been in contact with Commission staff regarding the filing of the 
Response, and expresses frustration at the dismissal of the matter. It appears the Complainant 
mistakenly mailed this letter to Public Service rather than the Commission. 

1

Certificate 
of 
Service 
included 
the 
following 
certified 
tracking 
number: 
9589 0710 5270 1409 2833 12 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0049 
PROCEEDING NO. 25F-0335EG 
5 
19. 
Given the confusion surrounding the receipt—or lack thereof—of the 
Complainant’s filings, and in the interest of ensuring procedural fairness and affording the 
Complainant a full opportunity to be heard, we find good cause to reopen this Proceeding pursuant 
to Rule 1504(b), 4 CCR 723-1. The Complainant’s Response to the Company’s Motion to Dismiss 
is attached as Attachment A to this Decision and is hereby entered into the record in this 
Proceeding. The ALJ may now consider the Complainant’s Response in determining how to move 
forward in this Proceeding and any next procedural steps. 
20. 
While we provide procedural flexibility for the Complainant in this instance, we 
remind the Complainant that Colorado law makes clear that pro se parties are bound by the same 
procedural rules as attorneys.2 We therefore expect all future filings to be timely received by the 
Commission. 
21. 
To avoid similar confusion moving forward, we encourage the Complainant to 
consider using the Commission’s E-Filings system for future filings in this Proceeding, which can 
be accessed using the following link: https://www.dora.state.co.us/pls/efi/EFI.homepage. 
If the Complainant has any questions on how to submit documents through E-Filings, he may 
contact the Commission’s E-Filings Administrator at alison.torvik@state.co.us. To the extent the 
Complainant prefers to use standard mail, we remind the Complainant that filings must be received 
by the Commission by the filing deadline.

A. 
The Commission Orders That:

Decision No. C26-0054-I

Statement

By this Decision the Commission schedules a public comment hearing to be held

Shutoff (“PSPS”) rules and to serve as a repository for public comments already received regarding

hearing and a Commissioner’s Information Meeting regarding the Public Service PSPS events that

ORDER 
A. 
It Is Ordered That: 
1.

I. 
BY THE COMMISSION 
A. 
Statement 
1. 
Through this Decision we grant, with clarifications, the Application for Rehearing, 
Reargument, or Reconsideration (“RRR”) of Decision No. C25-0892 that Trial Staff of the 
Public Utilities Commission (“Staff”), the Colorado Energy Office (“CEO”), and the Colorado 
Office of the Utility Consumer Advocate (“UCA”) (collectively, the “State Agencies”) filed on 
December 30, 2025. We also grant in part, with clarifications, and deny, in part, the RRR that 
Public Service Company of Colorado (“Public Service” or the “Company”) filed on 
December 30, 2025. Finally, we deny the RRR that CORE Electric Cooperative (“CORE”) filed 
on December 30, 2025. 
2. 
Through this Decision the Commission also grants the Motions for Leave to 
Respond filed on January 12, 2026, by Western Resource Advocates (“WRA”), the Environmental 
Justic Coalition (“EJC”), and the Conservation Coalition, respectively. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
3 
B. 
Background 
3. 
On November 10, 2025, Staff, CEO, UCA, and Public Service (the “Joint 
Petitioners”) filed a Joint Petition seeking a variance from Ordering Paragraphs 1 and 2 of Decision 
No. C18-0761,1 and any other decisions the Commission deems necessary, to modify the planned 
retirement date of Comanche Unit 2 (“Pueblo Unit 2”) from December 31, 2025, to 
December 31, 2026 (“Joint Petition”). 
4. 
In Decision No. C25-0892,2 the Commission granted, with modifications, the Joint 
Petition. In extending the life of Pueblo Unit 2, the Commission rejected requests from certain 
parties for a hearing, discovery, and answer testimony. The Commission reasoned that such due 
process will be afforded subsequently—particularly in the Step 2 application filing and when 
Public Service seeks to recover the costs associated with Unit 3’s outage—but that the Commission 
must move swiftly to allow Unit 2 to continue operating.3 As part of its decision to extend the life 
of Pueblo Unit 2, the Commission found that Unit 3’s prolonged, unplanned outage is the single 
justification for extending Unit 2.4 The Commission also stressed that there is no presumption of 
prudence for the repair of Unit 3 or operation of Unit 2. The Commission stated that 
“Public Service cannot assume that repairing Unit 3 is a prudent approach if better alternatives are 
available.”5 
5. 
In connection with Unit 2’s extension, the Commission directed additional 
reporting and future filings. To begin, the Commission largely adopted the two-step process put 
forth in the Joint Petition, consisting of the March 1, 2026 report and analysis (Step 1) and the 

1 Issued September 10, 2018, in Proceeding No. 16A-0396E. 
2 Issued December 10, 2025. 
3 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 64. 
4 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 65. 
5 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 70. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
4 
application filing the Company must file no later than June 1, 2026 (Step 2).6 The Commission 
went further than what the Joint Petitioners proposed, however, and required monthly reports 
containing additional information. One of the reporting requirements was for the Company to 
report any estimated material future capital costs for the repair of Unit 3 before such costs are 
obligated.7 
6. 
In addition to the reporting, the Commission placed operational limitations on 
Unit 2 and Unit 3 so that the two units together could not generate more than 3,942,000 MWh in 
2026. This 3,942,000 MWh limit is what Unit 3 could produce in 2026 given its 60 percent annual 
capacity factor limit agreed upon in the 2021 ERP.8 The Commission reasoned: “Given that 
Unit 2 and Unit 3 are now intended to work together to do the work that Unit 3 would have done 
but for its closure, it is reasonable to apply Unit 3’s operational limit from the 2021 ERP to both 
units.”9 The Commission noted that Public Service could file an appropriate request supported by 
testimony and other evidence if the Company had concerns with the 3,942,000 MWh limitation.10 
7. 
Chair Blank dissented from the operational limitations, opining that he would only 
require additional reporting on the collective operation of Unit 2 and Unit 3. Chair Blank expressed 
concerns about non-economic dispatch and how much the operational limitation would cost.11 
8. 
As referenced above, on December 30, 2025, the State Agencies, Public Service, 
and CORE each filed RRRs regarding Decision No. C25-0892.

9. 
On January 12, 2026, WRA, EJC, and Conservation Coalition each filed a Motion 
for Leave to Respond to the Company’s RRR. 
10. 
Public Service filed a Response in Opposition on January 20, 2026. 
C. 
Motions for Leave to Respond 
11. 
WRA, EJC, and Conservation Coalition each filed a Motion for Leave to Respond 
pursuant to Rule 1506(b), 4 Code of Colorado Regulations 723-1. Rule 1506(b) states that no 
response to an application for RRR may be filed expect upon motion and that any such motion 
must demonstrate one of the following: a material misrepresentation of a fact in the record; an 
incorrect statement or error of law; an attempt to introduce facts not in evidence; accident or 
surprise, which ordinary prudence could not have guarded against; or newly discovered facts or 
issues material for the moving party which that party could not, with reasonable diligence, have 
discovered prior to the time the application for RRR was filed. 
12. 
WRA seeks leave to respond because it contends Public Service’s RRR contains 
material misrepresentations of the Commission’s decision and incorrect statements of law 
regarding the operational limit for Pueblo Units 2 and 3. Specifically, WRA argues the Company 
mischaracterizes the limit as a “hard cap” requiring pre-approval, contrary to the Commission’s 
intent and the Updated Settlement Agreement (“USA”) in the Company’s 2021 Electric Resource 
Plan/Clean Energy Plan (“ERP/CEP”). 
13. 
EJC argues Public Service’s RRR include incorrect statements of law, material 
misrepresentations of fact, and new facts not in the Petition. EJC contends, for example, that the 
Company downplays emissions benefits, mischaracterizes the Commission’s decision, and 
introduces new proposals and information such as eliminating the 60% capacity factor limit for 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
6 
Unit 3 and reporting requirements for repair costs. EJC asserts these circumstances satisfy 
Rule 1506(b)’s criteria for granting leave to respond. 
14. 
Conservation Coalition alleges Public Service’s filing misrepresents the 
Commission’s decision, introduces facts not in evidence, and raises new arguments not contained 
in the Joint Petition. Conservation Coalition asserts the Company incorrectly claims the 
Commission invented a new operational limit, misstate settlement provisions, and for the first time 
requests removal of Unit 3’s generation cap. Conservation Coalition states these 
misrepresentations and surprises justify granting leave to respond. 
15. 
In the Company’s Response in Opposition, it contends none of the motions meet 
the standard under Rule 1506(b), and argues its RRR filing does not introduce new evidence or 
create unfair surprise, as the differences between Pueblo Units 2 and 3 and the absence of 
operational restrictions on Unit 2 in the USA are well-established facts of which the Commission 
can take administrative notice. Public Service further states its legal arguments regarding 
operational limits were foreseeable and that the issues raised in the motions can be addressed in 
the forthcoming June 1 application. Accordingly, Public Service requests that the Commission 
deny the motions for leave to respond 
16. 
We find good cause to grant the respective motions for leave to respond pursuant 
to Rule 1506(b). In this Proceeding, the motions reasonably assert that certain facts and 
issues—such as the estimated costs for Unit 3 repairs as well as expenditures already 
incurred—were raised for the first time in the Company’s RRR filings. Additionally, because this 
is an expedited Proceeding with limited opportunities for party input, granting these motions in 
this instance will allow for more fulsome participation in a fast-moving process. For these reasons,

the Commission finds it appropriate to exercise its discretion and grant the motions for leave to 
respond. 
D. 
Operational Limitations 
1. 
RRR Arguments 
17. 
In their Joint RRR, the State Agencies request the Commission remove the 
operational restriction on Unit 2 and Unit 3. They warn that unintended consequences of the 
operational limitation could result in significant costs being imposed on ratepayers through 
non-economic dispatch and the operational challenges of applying Unit 3’s capacity factor limit to 
the combination of Units 2 and 3 over different operational time periods. The State Agencies argue 
the Commission should defer to Public Service to implement the Unit 2 extension in line with its 
standard operating and dispatch procedures. The State Agencies express agreement with Chair 
Blank’s dissent from the operational limitation and his expressed concerns about non-economic 
dispatch and how much the operational limitation would cost.12 
18. 
The State Agencies note the Commission traditionally does not specifically direct 
the utility’s engineering practices, and the Commission should follow that practice here. 
They assert the operational restriction limits the Company’s ability to decide what is prudent and 
necessary in light of maintenance, safety and reliability concerns, and interferes with engineering 
and management practices that should be left to the Company. The State Agencies recommend 
that the Commission “squarely place the burden of prudent operations on the Company, including 
by granting it full control of unit operations.”13

13 Joint RRR at p. 3.

19. 
Moreover, the State Agencies express skepticism of the practical impact the 
operational limitations will have on reducing emissions. They argue that because Unit 2 is less 
than half the capacity of Unit 3, and Unit 3 is not expected to return to service before June 2026, 
it is unlikely that the combined operations would have a significant impact on emissions. 
In addition, the State Agencies note that if the constraint is hit, any resources the Company acquires 
on the market may be associated with increased emissions. 14 The State Agencies conclude that the 
continued operation of Unit 2 in 2026, without operational limitations, is the most cost-effective 
approach to providing needed electricity for the system. 
20. 
Public Service also challenges the operational limitations on Unit 2 and Unit 3. 
First, the Company argues the Decision’s operational limitations actually “inverts the settled, and 
previously Commission-approved, arrangement” for capacity factor limits for Unit 3 in the USA.15 
Public Service acknowledges that in the USA the Company agreed to operate Unit 3 at a maximum 
annual capacity factor of 60 percent for 2026. The Company argues, however, that this capacity 
factor limit was not an absolute bar on operating the unit if needed for reliability purposes. 
As support, the Company quotes paragraph 38 below from the USA: 
In the case of an extraordinary event(s) that the Company exceeds the 
maximum annual capacity factor for a given year, the Company will make 
a filing in its Electric Commodity Adjustment (“ECA”) annual prudence 
review to explain the circumstances that led to the need to exceed the 
maximum annual capacity factor.16 
21. 
Instead of the after-the-fact ECA review process agreed upon in the USA, 
Public Service argues the Commission appears to impose a hard cap on energy production from

which the Company cannot deviate without advance Commission approval. Public Service argues 
these changes to the USA are not workable or practical. 
22. 
The Company further argues the capacity limits agreed upon in the USA are subject 
to paragraph 41 of the USA that provides that “[p]rocuring adequate flexible, dispatchable 
generation is imperative to allow for the early reduced operations set forth in this proposal and a 
reliable system.”17 Public Service argues it has faced challenges in procuring dispatchable 
generation at the same time it has seen demand growth. 
23. 
In addition to its arguments relating to the USA, Public Service argues the 
operational limitations could be costly, have unintended consequences, and may not ultimately 
reduce emissions. The Company asserts that Chair Blank’s dissent is correct in that operating to a 
hard cap for Units 2 and 3 will result in non-economic dispatch if the operational limitation is 
binding. Public Service asserts the resulting additional costs could “easily range into the millions 
or even tens of millions of dollars….”18 Despite these additional costs, the Company warns the 
operational limitation may simply cause less efficient units more frequently. 
24. 
As for the unintended consequences, Public Service notes that Unit 2, which was 
built in the 1970s and nearing the end of its life, is much older than Unit 3. The Company asserts 
that both Unit 2 and Unit 3 are designed to run at stable power levels for long periods of time, and 
more frequent cycling can lead to malfunctions or damage—particularly with Unit 2.19 
The Company warns the operational limitation could jeopardize the Commission’s suggested 
option of running Unit 2 through 2030.

10 
25. 
Finally, Public Service argues in the alternative that if the Commission retains the 
operational limitation for Unit 2 and Unit 3, the Commission should at least follow the process set 
forth in the USA. Specifically, the Company requests the Commission eliminate the requirement 
that Public Service seek pre-approval to exceed the operational limitation and instead adopt the 
after-the-fact ECA review process in paragraph 38 of the USA. Public Service argues the USA’s 
ECA review process allows the Company to make operational decisions in real-time without 
day-to-day Commission oversight.20 
2. 
Responses to the RRRs 
26. 
In its Response, EJC argues the State Agencies and Public Service materially 
misrepresent the facts regarding the emissions benefits of the operational restrictions. EJC notes 
that coal-fired power plants typically emit greater amounts of air pollution and greenhouse gases 
than other types of generation resources. EJC therefore states that it is “quite doubtful” that 
electricity from other sources would have higher emissions.21 EJC further argues the other sources 
of electricity would not harm community members in Pueblo to the same extent: “the air pollution 
emitted by generation resources is not fungible, and the location, the amount, and the types of 
pollution emitted by generation facilities matter greatly to impacted communities.”22 In addition, 
EJC argues removing the operational constraint would be directly contrary to Senate Bill 21-272’s 
equity mandate. 
27. 
EJC also contests the State Agencies’ claim that the operational limit introduces 
complex and unplanned capacity factor limits. EJC argues the requirement that Public Service not 
generate more than 3.942 million MWh at the Pueblo coal plant in 2026 is not complex because it

Decision No. C26-0067

11 
provide Public Service significant discretion on how to operate the two units. EJC asserts it is not 
unplanned because the limit is derived from the USA. 
28. 
EJC asserts Public Service and the State Agencies, for the first time in RRR, seek 
to remove the 60 percent capacity limit on Unit 3. EJC notes the Joint Petition does not ask the 
Commission to eliminate or modify the 60 percent capacity factor limit for Unit 3 in 2026. In RRR, 
however, these parties now request the Commission allow Public Service to dispatch both units at 
its discretion, effectively eliminating the 60 percent capacity factor limit. EJC asserts this 
constitutes a “surprise” to EJC justifying EJC’s RRR Response.23 
29. 
Conservation Coalition argues the Commission should uphold the operational 
limitations on Unit 2 and Unit 3. As support, Conservation Coalition claims the Company now has 
additional capacity that was not available when the Joint Petition was filed. To be clear, 
Conservation Coalition does not request the Commission reject the extension of Unit 2 in light of

limitations.24

Conservation Coalition also argues Public Service’s statements in RRR undermine 
the assertion that in the absence of a generation limit, Units 2 and 3 would be dispatched

periods of time, that would impact the extent to which they can be economically dispatched in any

meaningful sense of that term. Conservation Coalition concludes that the Commission cannot grant

previously in Proceeding No. 21A-0141E. Conservation Coalition argues the Joint Petitioners

As for the arguments from the Joint Petitioners that the operational limit would

and Public Service in Proceeding No. 21A-0141E urging the Commission to approve those limits

The Company should not be allowed to use the unexpected outage at

Conservation Coalition maintains that this result would be inconsistent with the

36. 
Similar to EJC, Conservation Coalition argues that, for the first time in RRR, the 
Joint Petitioners ask the Commission to not apply the operational limitation to Unit 3. Conservation 
Coalition asserts this constitutes a procedurally improper request to revise the Phase I Decision

Finally, Conservation Coalition responds to Public Service’s critique that

Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
16 
also indicate the plant is not well-suited for our current system, which is defined by increasing 
amounts of variable generation from renewable resources. When we evaluate the prudency of 
Public Service’s operations of Unit 2 and Unit 3 (presumably in an ECA annual prudency review), 
we intend to examine whether Unit 2’s limitations, including its inability to cycle in the same way 
Unit 3 can, led to uneconomic dispatch of the Company’s system. We also find it appropriate to 
evaluate what would have occurred both in terms of costs and emissions had Unit 3 been available 
to operate as contemplated under the USA. 
42. 
In addition to the Company’s representations regarding Unit 2, we take seriously 
the arguments from the State Agencies that the Commission should allow Public Service to 
implement the Unit 2 extension in line with its standard operating and dispatch procedures and 
that the operational challenges of applying Unit 3’s capacity factor limit to the combination of 
Units 2 and 3 could result in significant costs on ratepayers. In particular, the Commission fully 
agrees with the following: “The State Agencies recommend that the Commission squarely place 
the burden of prudent operations on the Company, including by granting it full control of unit 
operations.”36 
43. 
We acknowledge the operational limitations may not require changes in how the 
Company would run Unit 2, especially prior to when Unit 3 comes back online. 
Ultimately, however, there is insufficient record to confidently predict how Public Service would 
respond to the operational limitations. Public Service may deem it necessary to cycle Unit 2 more 
frequently in the spring of 2026 to ensure that it has sufficient headroom to run Unit 3 as necessary 
during the summer. Arguments from EJC and Conservation Coalition to the contrary are 
unpersuasive. While both coal-fired plants were initially designed to run at stable power levels for 

36 Joint RRR at p. 3. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
17 
long periods of time, Unit 2 and Unit 3 are not the same. The fact that Public Service agreed in the 
USA to impose capacity factor restrictions on Unit 3 does not mean the Company’s concerns about 
applying those limitations on Unit 2 are unfounded. The burden of prudent operations must remain 
on the Company. 
44. 
The Commission agrees with Conservation Coalition and EJC that the Joint 
Petitioners’ arguments regarding emissions are unpersuasive. It is possible the alternative sources 
of electricity Public Service acquires to replace generation from Unit 3 and Unit 2 could have 
roughly the same emissions. However, the Joint Petitioners put forth no evidence to support this 
claim. It is just as possible the replacement generation could come from cleaner sources of 
electricity, such as renewables or gas. Even assuming the operational restrictions on Unit 2 and 
Unit 3 would reduce emissions during 2026, however, this factor alone does not overcome 
concerns about forcing Public Service to operate Unit 2 in a way that it was not designed to operate. 
45. 
EJC makes a legitimate point that air pollution is not fungible, and the types of 
pollution generating facilities emit matter greatly to the impacted communities. Nevertheless, this 
point does not justify imposing the operational restriction on Unit 2. In addition to the operational 
concerns regarding Unit 2, there is insufficient record to accurately estimate the relative impact of 
removing the operational limit on disproportionately impacted (“DI”) communities. It is possible 
the operational restriction could require the Company to run the Cherokee gas units, which are 
also in a DI community, at a higher capacity factor. While the emissions impact from coal are 
likely worse than the emissions impacts from gas units, such a high level analysis would overlook 
other important factors such as other sources of pollution the communities near the Cherokee units 
already face. While the Commission must consider how its decisions impact DI communities, there 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
18 
is insufficient record here to assume the operational limitation on Unit 2 will result in a net benefit 
to DI communities across Colorado. 
46. 
We clarify that we are reversing our decision to apply the operational limitation on 
Unit 2 at this time. Our decision to not impose operational limitations on Unit 2 is based on the 
limited record available in this Proceeding and the legitimate concerns the State Agencies and the 
Company raise regarding the operational impacts on Unit 2. This directive may change in future 
proceedings, consistent with the Joint Petitioners’ suggestions. In their Reply, the Joint Petitioners 
argue that “further evaluation of potential parameters is necessary before the Commission imposes 
such limits” and asserted that the two-step process will address future operations of Unit 2 and 
Unit 3.37 We therefore require Public Service to include in its June 1, 2026 step 2 application an 
analysis of what it would take to ensure the combined generation from Unit 2 and Unit 3 in 2026 
does not exceed the 3,942,000 MWh limit in the USA. Even if the timing of the Step 2 application 
impedes our ability to enact significant operational limitations for purposes of 2026, this analysis 
could provide useful information, especially if Public Service proposes to continue running 
Unit 2 after Unit 3 returns to service. 
47. 
Finally, we reaffirm the capacity factor limitations for Unit 3 agreed upon in the 
USA remain in place. While we decline to include, at this time, Unit 2’s operations in the 
calculation of Unit 3’s capacity factor, this in no way removes the 60 percent capacity factor 
limitation on Unit 3 for 2026, the 50 percent capacity factor limitation for 2027, nor the 33 percent 
capacity factor limitation beginning in 2029. The Joint Petitions have not justified modifying the 
USA to remove the restrictions on Unit 3. Finally, we direct that the capacity factor limitation for 
Unit 3 in 2026 shall be prorated by the amount of time Unit 3 was offline. Thus, if Unit 3 is only 

37 Joint Reply at p. 5. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
19 
online for six months during 2026, the 60 percent capacity factor limitation must be calculated 
based only on those six months. 
E. 
Restrictions on Repair Costs 
1. 
RRR Arguments 
48. 
Public Service requests reconsideration of the Commission’s directives that 
material future capital costs for Unit 3’s repair be reported to the Commission before such costs 
are obligated. In particular, the Company asks the Commission to strike the phrases “before such 
costs are obligated” and “before they are obligated,” in paragraphs 73 and 74 of the Decision. 
49. 
As context, Public Service’s RRR reveals the Company’s estimated cost for Unit 3 
repairs,38 notes that some costs have already been incurred, and adds that insurance may cover 
some of the expenses. Public Service asserts that bringing Unit 3 back online for summer 2026 
required the Company to begin work before the report and application process contemplated in the 
Joint Petition. The Company argues it “scoped and understood the repairs before making the 
decision to proceed, and made its decision to proceed with repairing Unit 3 based on the totality 
of the circumstances.”39. 
50. 
Public Service states that it accepts the Commission’s warnings that the Company’s 
decisions regarding Unit 3 will be closely scrutinized and that no presumption of prudence applies 
with respect to any repair costs. However, the Company argues that requiring the Company to 
make regulatory filings for every contract signing and change order relating to potential repair 
work would delay work, which in turn would likely extend the outage and raise costs for customers. 
Public Service notes that under the Phase I Decision in the 2021 ERP/CEP, Public Service is 

38 Public Service designates these costs as confidential. 
39 Public Service RRR at p. 9. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
20 
already required to report on unplanned Unit 3 outages with associated costs above $30 million.40 
Instead of being required to report material repair costs before they are obligated, the Company 
offers to provide updated estimated costs on a monthly basis, specifying the costs that have already 
been obligated and any updates on insurance coverage. 
2. 
RRR Responses 
51. 
EJC asserts that in Public Service’s RRR the Company informs the Commission 
for the first time in this case that it “is proceeding with repair of Unit 3” and has already incurred 
repair costs. EJC states these are new facts that were not included in the Joint Petition. EJC argues 
the “fact that Public Service has already spent money repairing Unit 3 only underscores the need 
for the Commission to exercise heightened scrutiny and oversight of the Company’s actions.”41 
EJC argues the most reasonable and cost-effective path forward is likely for Public Service to not 
repair Unit 3 and to only modestly extend the life of Unit 2. EJC argues Public Service should not 
be allowed to preemptively impede the Commission’s review process by spending significant 
amounts of money to repair Unit 3 before the Step 2 proceeding begins. 
52. 
Conservation Coalition similarly argues the Commission should retain the 
requirement to inform the Commission of material expenses before they are obligated. 
Conservation Coalition asserts the reporting directive will not delay the Unit 3 repairs. 
Conservation Coalition reasons the Commission did not impose “a CPCN-type requirement to 
obtain a Commission decision prior to obligating funds—only that the Commission must be 
informed of material expenditures prior to their obligation.”42 Conservation Coalition argues 
imposing a mere reporting requirement in advance of obligating material funds will not cause any 

40 Public Service RRR at p. 10. 
41 EJC RRR Response at p. 12. 
42 Public Service RRR at p. 19. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
21 
material delay. They add the requirement to report material costs before they are obligated enables 
the Commission to have additional insight into those expenses and at least leaves open the 
possibility of initiating some additional process if those costs were to reach a level that triggers 
concern. 
3. 
Findings and Conclusions 
53. 
We grant Public Service’s RRR on this point and accept the Company’s offer to 
provide updated estimated costs on a monthly basis, specifying the costs that have already been 
obligated and any updates on insurance coverage. Granting the Company’s RRR would result in 
requirements that are more in line with the existing reporting requirements from the 2021 
ERP/CEP, which may be appropriate based on the Company’s estimated repair costs. We further 
agree with Public Service that it is not in customers’ interest or the interest of the system to require 
the Company to delay repair work in order to file the appropriate reports. 
54. 
While we agree with Conservation Coalition that Decision No. C25-0892 does not 
impose a CPCN-type requirement for Public Service to obtain Commission approval prior to 
obligating funds, there is insufficient information to draw a conclusion that this reporting 
requirement will not cause material delays. More fundamentally, it is unclear whether the 
possibility of initiating some additional process is worth obtaining the reporting beforehand, as 
opposed to the Company’s offer to update estimated repair costs on a monthly basis. 
55. 
Finally, we observe that Public Service has already decided to proceed with the 
repair of Unit 3.43 We reiterate that Public Service has not requested—and the Commission does 
not provide—any assurance that the Company’s decision to repair Unit 3 is prudent. Public Service 
remains at risk of not recovering from ratepayers the costs incurred to repair Unit 3 if the Company 

43 Public Service RRR at p. 9 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
22 
fails to meet its burden in a future proceeding that it acted prudently. In a similar vein, we disagree 
with EJC’s suggestion that allowing Public Service to spend money on Unit 3 prior to reporting 
estimated costs will somehow impede the Commission’s ability to review the prudence of 
Public Service’s decisions. 
F. 
CORE’s RRR 
56. 
CORE states its RRR “focuses solely on the Commission’s decisions around the 
costs and prudency of repairs and operations of Unit 3.”44 CORE argues the prudency of the 
repairs, recovery of the costs of those repairs, and future operations of Unit 3 are not properly 
before the Commission. 
57. 
CORE asserts the Commission improperly enlarged the scope of the Proceeding 
when it considered the prudency of Unit 3 repairs and obligations. CORE notes that in the Notice 
of Petition Filed, the Commission provided that the Petition was for “a variance from Decision 
No. C18-9761 relating to the planned retirement date of Comanche Unit 2.”45 According to CORE, 
the Notice does not notify the public that the Commission would use this Proceeding to engage in 
the prudency of repairs and operations of Unit 3. CORE thus concludes the Commission’s 
“engagement in the prudency of repairs and operations of Unit 3 during this proceeding is 
improper.”46 CORE asserts the Commission’s questions regarding the prudence of Unit 3 
operations and repairs and the on-going Unit 3 reporting reflect the intent of the Commission to 
continue to evaluate the prudency of such expenditures even though this is outside the scope of the 
proceeding. 

44 CORE RRR at p. 3. 
45 CORE RRR at p. 10. 
46 CORE RRR at p. 10. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
23 
58. 
CORE also argues the Commission lacks sufficient evidence to make Unit 3 
prudency determinations. CORE acknowledges the Commission’s statement that disallowing 
Unit 3 costs would be premature but argues the Commission’s reporting requirements indicate that 
it plans to determine the prudency of repairs and operations of Unit 3 during this proceeding. 
CORE argues that without more process, such as written testimony, discovery, and hearings, the 
Commission “should not engage in, nor give the appearance that it is weighing the prudency of 
repairs and operations of Unit 3.”47 
59. 
CORE explains that energy market participants regularly monitor Commission 
decisions to further understand industry oversight and compliance and assess regulatory certainty. 
CORE asserts that weighing the prudence of Unit 3’s repairs and operations creates risks to the 
financial well-being of the owners of Unit 3.48 
60. 
CORE further argues the decision to extend the retirement date of Unit 2 does not 
require the Commission to determine the prudency of repairs and operations of Unit 3. CORE 
argues the Joint Petition did not seek cost recovery for Unit 2’s extension or Unit 3’s repairs, but 
the Commission repeatedly expressed concerns over the unknown costs and the prudency of 
repairing Unit 3.49 
61. 
Finally, CORE asserts the Commission failed to provide the necessary 
constitutional due process protections of adequate notice and meaningful opportunity to be heard. 
If the Commission rejects CORE’s RRR and engages in the prudency of repairs and operations of 

47 CORE RRR at p. 12. 
48 CORE RRR at p. 12. 
49 CORE RRR at p. 13. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
24 
Unit 3, CORE requests the Commission’s allow for evidentiary hearings, discovery, and answer 
testimony along with a sufficient evidentiary record for this proceeding.50 
1. 
Findings and Conclusions 
62. 
We reject CORE’s RRR. In CORE’s own words, its RRR “focuses solely on the 
Commission’s decisions around the costs and prudency of repairs and operations of Unit 3.”51 
Nevertheless, CORE fails to cite a single prudency determination the Commission made regarding 
Unit 3. Decision No. C25-0892 contains none. 
63. 
CORE seems to argue the Commission is restricted to the precise words contained 
within the Notice without accounting for the fact that the Notice is only required to provide “a 
brief description” of the application or petition.52 Under CORE’s logic, any claim or relief filed in 
a petition or application that the Commission does not expressly recite in its notice cannot be 
adjudicated. This would require extensive Commission notices. In fact, the Notice in this 
Proceeding appropriately summarizes the purpose and scope of the Joint Petition and directs the 
public to the actual Joint Petition. 
64. 
CORE’s remaining arguments fail once the issues set forth in the Joint 
Petition—as opposed to only the particular words in the Notice—are considered. For instance, the 
Joint Petition proposes a two-step process, including a Step 1 report on March 1, 2026. As set forth 
in the Joint Petition: 
This report will include an update on the repair and return to service status 
of Comanche Unit 3, including forecasted cost of repairs, any resource 
options identified in collaborative work with the Joint Petitioners for 
potential near-term resource adequacy benefits, and other analysis relevant 
to the four areas outlined above. It will also include an initial plan to address 

50 CORE RRR at p. 14. 
51 CORE RRR at p. 3. 
52 Rule 1206(b)(IV). 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
25 
on-going needs considering all available options, including not only plant 
extensions, but also expedited resource additions and demand-side options, 
with further refinement in Step 2.53 
65. 
More broadly, the Joint Petition states the proposed two-step process creates an 
orderly process as the Company “assesses the future operation of Comanche Unit 2, Comanche 
Unit 3, and other resource options.”54 Also, the Joint Petition argues that Unit 3’s outage is not the 
only justification for Unit 2’s extension.55 
66. 
Considering the proposals and arguments set forth in the Joint Petition, the 
Commission did not improperly enlarge the scope of this Proceeding. The Joint Petition itself 
contemplates considerable reporting, including on Unit 3’s repair costs. While the Commission 
added to the reporting the Joint Petition proposed, these additions fall squarely within the issues 
initially raised in the Joint Petition. 
67. 
Apart from the additional reporting, CORE argues throughout the RRR the 
Commission improperly “engaged” or “weighed” the prudence of Unit 3’s operations and repairs. 
There is nothing improper about the Commission discussing the possibility that Public Service’s 
conduct regarding Unit 3 is imprudent and directing additional reporting along those lines. This is 
especially true where the Commission expressly rejected requests from other parties to proactively 
prohibit cost recovery associated with repairing Unit 3.56

54 Joint Petition at p. 8. 
55 Joint Petition at p. 4.

Decision No. C26-0067

G. 
Reporting on Replacement Energy Costs 
1. 
Public Service’s RRR 
68. 
In its RRR, Public Service also seeks clarification regarding the following directive 
in paragraph 74 to provide monthly reports on the replacement energy costs associated with 
Unit 3’s outage: 
Any additional future or actual costs incurred related to the outage of Unit 
3, including but not limited to repair costs and replacement energy costs, for 
which Public Service may seek recovery from Colorado ratepayers, along 
with a functional breakdown of the costs and an explanation for why the 
costs were incurred57 
69. 
Public Service argues it “does not know in real time, and cannot report on a 
monthly basis, the exact replacement costs for any particular outage.”58 Instead, the Company 
explains such calculations require replacement power modeling similar to what was done in annual 
ECA prudence review or the recent review of the Cabin Creek upgrades. Public Service asserts 
that replacement power modeling takes multiple months to conduct and significant employee time. 
70. 
The Company states it will commit to filing full replacement power cost modeling 
for the Unit 3 outage in the ECA annual prudence review proceeding for 2026 to be filed in 2027 
or in an appropriate stand-alone proceeding. The Company further commits to include in its 
monthly reports the actual bilateral energy and capacity purchases in a similar format to what is 
provided in the annual ECA prudence reviews. 
2. 
Findings and Conclusions 
71. 
The Commission grants Public Service’s RRR on this point based on the 
Company’s representations that it does not know in real time the replacement costs for any 

57 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 74. 
58 Public Service RRR at p. 15. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
27 
particular outage and that each modeling run necessary to calculate this amount takes multiple 
months. We accept the Company’s alternative offer to include in the monthly reports the 
Company’s actual bilateral energy and capacity purchases. In addition, we direct Public Service to 
include the full replacement power cost modeling for the Unit 3 outage in whatever proceeding 
the Company attempts to establish the prudency of such costs. If this occurs via the ECA, the 
modeling must be filed in the 2027 annual prudency review proceeding for 2026 costs. 
H. 
Justification for Unit 2’s Extension and Resource Adequacy Concerns 
1. 
Public Service’s RRR 
72. 
In Decision No. C25-0892 we found “that Unit 3’s prolonged, unplanned outage is 
the single justification for extending Unit 2.”59 The Commission noted that, prior to Unit 3’s 
breakdown, the Company never suggested that it would need to extend the retirement date of 
Unit 2 because of factors such as supply chain and geopolitical issues, changes to the Company’s 
resource accreditation methodology, and increasing peak demand. 
73. 
Public Service disputes this finding in its RRR.60 Public Service asserts that just 
because the Company had not previously asked for a coal unit’s extension, this does not compel 
the conclusion that there is only one factor influencing the need to extend Unit 2.61 Public Service 
proffers four reasons why the Company never previously raised Unit 2’s extension. For example, 
the Company states that “advocating for coal extensions would have induced strong opposition 
that would have distracted form the main focus of the Company’s resource planning 
proceedings.”62 Public Service also states the Commission’s current bench has repeatedly signaled 

59 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 65. 
60 Public Service RRR at p. 2. 
61 Public Service RRR at p. 6. 
62 Public Service RRR at pp. 6-7. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
28 
that it disfavors coal generation, so the Commission should not be surprised that the Company did 
not bring forward a Unit 2 extension in the earlier ERP proceedings. The Company adds: “And it 
would be a stretch for anyone to claim that, even if the Company had proposed an extension of an 
aging coal unit in those proceedings to gain megawatts on a loads and resources table, the 
Commission would have approved such a proposal.”63 
74. 
Public Service also spends significant time in its RRR arguing that 
Commission-caused delays regarding the new-build CTs the Company bid into the 2021 ERP 
contributed to the current resource adequacy situation. For instance, the Company asserts that 
“after 15 months of regulatory process following the Company’s 120-Day Report, the Company’s 
portfolio was reduced from 600 MW of CTs to 400 MW.”64 Public Service suggests that 
Commission actions regarding Bid 1000 and Bid 0989 (two Company-owned thermal projects bid 
into the 2021 ERP/CEP) contributed to the current resource adequacy situation and the need to 
extend Unit 2.65 
2. 
Findings and Conclusions 
75. 
We reject the Company’s RRR arguments and reaffirm that that Unit 3’s prolonged, 
unplanned outage is the single justification that has been demonstrated here for the extension of 
Unit 2.66 The various reasons Public Service references in its RRR for why it did not request an 
extension of Unit 2 earlier are unpersuasive. If indeed there was a need to extend Unit 2 prior to 
Unit 3’s breakdown, these arguments suggest that the Company chose not to raise the issue until 
there was an emergency. A more reasonable explanation is that during the prior ERP proceedings, 

63 Public Service RRR at p. 7. 
64 Public Service RRR at p. 5. 
65 Public Service RRR at p. 3. 
66 Chair Blank dissents from this part and would instead find that given changing federal policy, 
Unit 3’s unplanned outage is the “primary” justification for extending Unit 2. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
29 
Public Service was planning to reliably serve load in 2026 without using Unit 2. While extending 
Unit 2 would have allowed the Company “to gain megawatts on a loads and resources table,” 
Public Service anticipated it could reliably serve load without doing so. This changed in the fall of 
2025 when Unit 3 broke down and the Company unexpectedly lost 415 MW of accredited capacity 
for an extended period of time. 
76. 
In addition, we disagree with the Company’s characterization of the Commission’s 
resource adequacy proceedings. In the 2021 ERP/CEP the Commission’s approved portfolio 
included more thermal resources than the Company’s preferred portfolio, and we rejected 
arguments in RRR to reduce the amount of thermal resources, reasoning that doing so could risk 
reliability. While one of the thermal resources in the approved Phase II portfolio failed, the 
Commission established a backup selection process by which the Company could have established 
Bid 1000 as the replacement.67 Acknowledging the need to be able to quickly shift to backup 
projects, the Commission also invited the Company to file a petition for waiver of the backup bid 
selection process as circumstances require.68 The Company elected not to use these procedures but 
instead waited until its Motion to Approve the CEP Delivery to address Bid 1000. 
77. 
More broadly, the Commission has set up flexible resource acquisition processes 
and has been responsive to stakeholder requests to pursue novel regulatory processes to address 
quickly changing circumstances and rising costs. These include the backup bid selection process, 
the CEP Delivery Plan, the interim just transition solicitation and its Phase II Framework, the 
near-term procurement process, and this current proceeding in which the Commission achieved 
the accelerated timeframe for a written decision one month after the Joint Petition was filed. 

67 Phase II RRR Decision at ¶ 77. 
68 Phase II RRR Decision at ¶ 70. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
30 
78. 
Rather than Commission-caused delays, the relevant history regarding the 
Company-owned thermal bids seems more about risk allocation and the implementation of the 
cost-to-construct performance incentive mechanism in a rising cost environment. In retrospect, 
Public Service needed to reprice its thermal bids given the Company could not come anywhere 
close to constructing the thermal projects at their original bid prices. It appears this may now be 
possible through novel regulatory processes such as the CEP Delivery Plan and the near term 
procurement. 
79. 
Regardless, a detailed history of Bid 1000 and Bid 0989 appears irrelevant to this 
Proceeding. As originally bid, these projects were not expected to come online until 2027 or later. 
Even if the Commission had approved these bids in the initial Phase II Decision, the projects would 
not have been available to help replace the capacity lost when Unit 3 broke down in the fall of 
2025. The Company would still need to find replacement energy and capacity for 2026. 
80. 
As for the issue of resource adequacy more broadly, back in Phase I of the 2021 
ERP/CEP, the Commission found: 
[I]t is in the public interest to have robust and updated contingency planning 
that includes gas-fired resources such as CTs that are fully permitted 
(including the air quality permit) and on standby—although not authorized 
for construction—should they be needed. The record in Phase I seems to 
indicate this could be as much as 400-500 MW of CTs. . . .69 
81. 
We note this 400-500 MW of standby thermal resources was in addition to the 
roughly 600 MW of thermal capacity the Commission approved in its Phase II Decision.70 
Given the significant uncertainties surrounding the load forecast, unit availability, supply chain 
bottlenecks, and changing federal policy, creating optionality to reduce delays and maintain 

69 Decision No. C22-0559, issued September 21, 2022, at ¶ 59 in Proceeding No. 21A-0141E. 
70 Decision No. C22-0559 at ¶ 60 (noting that because the standby CTs are backup resources, they 
will not affect the Company’s resource need). 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
31 
resource adequacy is essential. There is no indication the Company has pursued such standby 
thermal assets with air quality permits, but we reiterate our request first made in September 2022 
that Public Service do so sooner rather than later. 
II. 
ORDER 
A. 
The Commission Orders That: 
1. 
The Application for Rehearing, Reargument, or Reconsideration of Decision No. 
C25-0892 that Trial Staff of the Public Utilities Commission, the Colorado Energy Office, and the 
Colorado Office of the Utility Consumer Advocate filed on December 30, 2025, is granted with 
clarifications, consistent with the discussion above. 
2. 
The Application for Rehearing, Reargument, or Reconsideration of Decision No. 
C25-0892 that Public Service Company of Colorado filed on December 30, 2025, is granted, in 
part, with clarifications, and denied, in part, consistent with the discussion above. 
3. 
The Application for Rehearing, Reargument, or Reconsideration of Decision No. 
C25-0892 that CORE Electric Cooperative filed on December 30, 2025, is denied. 
4. 
The Motion for Leave to Respond filed by Western Resource Advocates on 
January 12, 2026, is granted. 
5. 
The Motion for Leave to Respond filed by the Environmental Justice Coalition on 
January 12, 2026, is granted. 
6. 
The Motion for Leave to Respond filed by the Conservation Coalition on 
January 12, 2026, is granted.

Decision No. R26-0079-I

of its Commission-issued Letter of Authority with its Intervention. 
9. 
On December 23, 2025, the Commission deemed the Amended Application 
complete and referred this matter to an Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) by minute entry. 
10. 
As relevant here, on January 14, 2026, the ALJ acknowledged Epic and iLIMO as 
intervening parties and established a January 29, 2026 deadline by which Aspire and Colorado

until after the deadline to file their Letters of Authority.8 
11. 
On January 28, 2026, Aspire filed a copy of its Commission-issued Letter of 
Authority for its CPCN Permit No. 55865.

On January 29, 2026, Colorado Sightseer filed Commission Decision No. C17-

“Decision No. C17-0584”). Colorado Sightseer did not file a copy of its Commission-issued Letter
